item.title: Elon Musk, Delta Airlines and a Feud Over In-Flight Wi-Fi
item.description:
Airplane Wi-Fi has long been slow and balky. But airlines are racing to change that.

Hoping that faster, more reliable internet access will help them attract and retain customers, many carriers are upgrading their planes to use Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. On Thursday, American Airlines said it would outfit more than 1,000 planes with Starlink.

But Delta Air Lines has chosen not to go with Starlink, which has upset Mr. Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

Mr. Musk said last month that Delta’s chief executive would “lose his job” for choosing Amazon’s satellite service, and he earlier attacked the top executive of Ryanair, the European carrier, for snubbing Starlink, too. This week, he said Indian oligarchs were blocking Starlink there, which he called a “a crime against the people of India.”

Lufthansa was the first commercial airline to offer in-flight internet access in 2004, using a service developed by Boeing. But Boeing shut down the project just two years later.

Other providers filled the void, and U.S. airlines started to offer Wi-Fi in the late 2000s. But few passengers used those services, which were often expensive, slow and unreliable. Over the years, the costs started to fall.

In 2023, Delta eliminated Wi-Fi fees for members of the company’s loyalty program. JetBlue Airways had been offering free internet access for years — but Delta kicked off an industry shift.

Many airlines offer free internet service to passengers who sign up for frequent flier programs. The programs allow the companies to collect more information about travelers and to encourage them to buy more tickets and sign up for credit cards.

At an industry conference last month, Robert Isom, the chief executive of American, said the airline was expanding its loyalty program at record rates. “A lot of that is driven by the free Wi-Fi,” he said.

Executives also say they are switching to Starlink because the earlier internet services they offered were subpar. This summer, executives at Alaska Airlines said customer satisfaction was about 20 percent higher on flights with Starlink.

But some industry experts say that most travelers pick airlines for many reasons and that Wi-Fi is not the most important one.

“People who are going to fly a lot in the future are going to self-select and gradually find the right program that fits best for them,” said Jay Sorensen, who runs IdeaWorksCompany, an aviation industry consulting firm. “You can’t really create that.”

That doesn’t mean Wi-Fi is irrelevant. Like soft drinks and snacks, internet access has become an expectation among passengers, Mr. Sorensen said.

Most major U.S. airlines upgrading to high-speed Wi-Fi are going with Starlink, whose satellites orbit closer to Earth than older satellites.

American, Alaska, United and Southwest Airlines have selected Starlink. But Delta, the most profitable U.S. airline, and JetBlue have chosen Amazon Leo, a satellite service that is not yet available.

After Delta announced the partnership this year, Mr. Musk said the airline “wanted to make it painful, difficult and expensive for their customers.” Last week, he said Delta’s chief, Ed Bastian, had made an error that could cost him his position. Mr. Musk was responding to an unverified report that Mr. Bastian had said it was not wise to work with Mr. Musk.

In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. Bastian disputed that report.

“I wouldn’t say that in a public setting or a private setting,” he said. “What we said is that we’re not working with Starlink because we decided to go a different direction.”

On Friday, Delta reported $20.2 billion in revenue for the third quarter of the year, during the three months ending in September, a company record.

SpaceX and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment.

This isn’t the first time Mr. Musk has criticized executives, politicians and others he disagrees with. In addition to Mr. Bastian, his targets have included Jeff Bezos, the executive chair of Amazon, and the chief executive of Ryanair, Michael O’Leary.

Delta’s decision to use Leo could be risky. While other airlines have already begun offering Starlink service on some flights, Delta won’t begin installing Amazon’s service until 2028.

That doesn’t mean Delta isn’t making upgrades, Mr. Bastian said. One of the airline’s current internet providers, Viasat, recently launched two new satellites that will “change the game for our customers,” he said.

Mr. Bastian has said Delta chose Amazon because it will cost the airline less than Starlink and because the airline hopes to provide customers other perks from Amazon. Delta has been profitable in recent years partly because customers like its credit cards, lounges and partnerships with other companies. For example, Delta’s customers can earn miles by buying coffee at Starbucks and hailing rides on Uber.

“We’ll be working very closely with them to bring new experiences to customers,” he said of Amazon. “It’s not just about the Wi-Fi; it’s what you do with the Wi-Fi.”

item.title: America’s Favorite Fruit Is Being Bruised by the Iran War
item.description:
The war in Iran has rippled through the global economy in many ways, pushing up prices for oil, fertilizer and other products. It has also created challenges for America’s most popular fruit: bananas.

The banana business has long been an underappreciated feat of logistics. It involves transporting a fragile and finicky fruit thousands of miles from the tropics, only to be sold for less than a quarter each. And it’s a business that is even trickier of late as the war raises the costs of fuel and other materials banana producers need.

That has put even more financial pressure on banana producers, who operate with thin margins and have little ability to raise prices. Compounding the industry’s problems are the threat of disease, climate change, tariffs and an exceptionally severe El Niño this year.

The banana might be America’s most unassuming fruit, a cheaply priced staple of smoothies and school cafeterias. It is the most consumed fruit in the United States, with Americans eating around 80 bananas a year, on average.

But bananas make little profit for grocery stores or the companies growing them. Instead, stores price them cheaply to draw shoppers in the door. The average price of bananas in the United States — about 65 cents a pound in August — has changed little over the last decade, despite rising costs.

“Everything is costing more money,” said Danny Dumas, a senior vice president at Del Monte North America. “If you ask me, it is a crisis.”

Even so, Del Monte, like the other major banana producers, Chiquita, Dole and Fyffes, continues to bring massive quantities of fruit to the United States.

In a port outside Philadelphia this summer, cranes and trucks busily unloaded hundreds of refrigerated containers from the Del Monte Spirit, a hulking ship that stretches two football fields long and had traveled more than 2,000 miles from Central America.

The ship, one of seven in Del Monte’s fleet, contained about 7 percent of the bananas that would be brought into the United States that week, supplying an area stretching from Iowa to North Carolina and Nova Scotia. The crew had just 40 hours to empty the ship’s cargo — millions of bananas from Guatemala and Costa Rica — before it would sail back for the next week’s pickup.

To understand the impact of the war, The New York Times traced the journey of a container of bananas from that ship over roughly 2,500 miles, from the plantation where it was grown to a Pennsylvania grocery store.

Some bananas on the Del Monte Spirit were grown in Tiquisate, a farm-dotted flood plain on the Pacific coast of Guatemala. Once carefully packed to avoid bruising, they were driven more than 250 miles in a refrigerated truck to Santo Tomás de Castilla, a port on Guatemala’s Caribbean coast.

The Spirit then carried them to Gloucester City, N.J., where Del Monte unloads up to 300,000 boxes of bananas a week. The company ships them directly to retailers or sends them to its own ripening facilities, which slowly increase the temperature and introduce ethylene gas so the bananas turn a perfect, unblemished yellow on your kitchen counter.

While many farmers and food sellers have seen costs increase because of the war, bananas have been hit harder because they are transported long distances and must be kept carefully refrigerated.

The price of diesel — needed to power Del Monte’s fleet of refrigerated trucks — has risen about 70 percent in the United States since the war started seven months ago, peaking at over $6 a gallon. Prices have also surged for the bunker fuel for Del Monte’s ships, and for the fuel for farmers’ irrigation systems in Central and South America.

The fertilizer that banana plantations depend on has also become more expensive, since much of it is made from natural gas coming from the Middle East. And the higher cost of shipping has spilled over into other products, like cardboard and plastic packaging and the chemicals that farmers spray on bananas to prevent disease.

Although the Trump administration has repeatedly pronounced the war with Iran over, the cease-fires have so far not held.

Transits out of the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz — which formerly helped to move about a third of the world’s fertilizer and a quarter of its seaborne oil — are still a small fraction of what they were. While more oil is flowing out of the Middle East than before, global oil prices have repeatedly breached $100 per barrel over the last seven months.

“Across the supply chain, everything depends on energy,” Mohammed Abbas, Del Monte’s president, said in an interview.

Del Monte grows some of its own bananas and buys others from farmers. Banana companies worry that higher prices may cause farmers to forgo fertilizer and disease-treating chemicals, resulting in a smaller crop next year. Some Central American farmers are already switching to pineapples.

Rising costs could also sap the industry’s ability to invest in disease-resistant varieties. The banana as Americans know it — a genetically homogeneous strain called Cavendish — is at risk from fungi and viruses that are spreading through South America.

While there are hundreds of varieties of bananas, ranging from the silvery-blue Ice Cream banana to the purplish Red Dacca, many Americans encounter only the Cavendish. Until the 1950s, Americans ate a variety called Gros Michel, a plumper, sweeter banana with a thick skin suited for shipping, and a flavor profile that lives on in banana-flavored candy.

But a fungus called Panama disease decimated the Gros Michel by the 1960s. Farmers turned to the Cavendish, first cultivated by an English gardener in the 1800s. Virtually all bananas consumed in the United States descend from that single English plant.

As farmers adapted, so did fungus. Another strain of Panama disease now targets Cavendish bananas in Southeast Asia and South America. It can survive in soil for decades, permanently wiping out farms.

Companies are quietly researching genetic alternatives in case the global supply collapses, an effort requiring significant investment. Del Monte declined to comment on its program.

Miguel Angel Morales, a small producer in northern Peru, said Panama disease had wiped out one in three banana-growing valleys in his region, forcing him and others to relocate their farms. The region produced 12 containers of bananas five years ago, but farmers now fill only one.

Stress from the war in Iran has compounded those problems. Mr. Morales said that his costs had jumped 25 to 30 percent this year, and that there was little support from banks or the government.

He had not yet raised his prices because annual contracts locked them in. Eventually, he thought, consumers in wealthier regions should pay more.

“If production costs increase, it’s logical that banana prices should increase, right?” he asked.

Yet an undisputed truth — at least among banana executives — is that the effort they put into their product has little relation to its price.

For decades, grocery stores have approached bananas as they do other “loss leaders” — pricing the fruit cheaply to get customers in the door. The industry structure, in which several companies compete to sell a largely identical product, also leaves banana producers with little power to raise their prices.

Banana companies have also developed highly efficient supply chains that shaved internal costs from farm to store — a strategy brutally perfected by the United Fruit Company, which turned large parts of Central America into company-run territory in the early 1900s.

The result is that the banana, despite being fragile and shipped long distances, is typically sold for as little as 15 cents each.

Adjusted for inflation, the average price of a pound of bananas in the United States has fallen roughly by half in the last 40 years. In the second quarter, Del Monte’s margin on bananas was just 2.3 percent.

“I always used to say that we are a nonprofit business,” said Juan Alarcon, the chief executive of Fyffes North America.

Banana companies also struggled last year with costs from tariffs, until the Trump administration exempted some food that is not locally grown in November.

Companies have also contended with a shortage of truck drivers, in part because the Trump administration stripped more than 30,000 drivers of commercial licenses.

The price at which many producers sell bananas is fixed by long-term contracts, some of which expire in December. But it’s not clear how much grocery stores will allow prices to rise.

Tom Stenzel, managing director of the Banana Association of North America, said it was “almost a mythology” among retailers that they couldn’t raise the price of bananas, the way they could for produce grown much closer to stores.

“I don’t want to throw my apple brothers under the bus,” Mr. Stenzel said, but apples are more expensive and take less effort to grow and ship. The banana industry’s ability to absorb costs is “at a breaking point,” he added.

“What else can you buy in a grocery store for 25 cents?” he asked.

Mitra Taj contributed reporting from Peru, and Jody García from Guatemala.

item.title: World’s Energy Order Tested Again as Iran War’s Reach Extends Further
item.description:
The intensifying war in the Middle East threatens to further strain a weary energy industry that has already endured waves of disruptions and could test a market resilience built on a series of extraordinary government and private-sector measures.

Over the weekend, the Iranian-backed Houthi militia attacked an international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, including one strike that killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds. It was the deadliest attack in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February and brought the war to the center of the Middle East’s oil industry.

The attack forced the temporary suspension of operations at the airport just as energy executives and government officials were set to arrive in Riyadh for a major business and policy conference. The event, the World ⁠Petroleum Congress, proceeded as planned, although some attendees were diverted to other airports and others, including the U.S. energy secretary, Chris Wright, and ministers from Italy and Japan, addressed the conference by video link.

Many oil industry leaders — including the chief executives of Exxon Mobil and BP — canceled their trips to Saudi Arabia, according to two industry officials who were not authorized to discuss executive schedules.

In remarks on Monday, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, acknowledged that recent attacks had “tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience.”

Meanwhile, oil tankers are facing persistent peril while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow passage between Iran and Oman that was a fairly uncomplicated excursion before the war. At least 16 vessels have been attacked this month.

The widening of the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen, amid no public signs of a diplomatic resolution between the United States and Iran, underscores the potent two-front threat facing energy infrastructure in an area crucial to global supplies of crude oil and its many byproducts like diesel and gasoline.

Just last month, oil exports from the region started increasing to nearly their prewar levels. More ships were getting out of the Strait of Hormuz, close to the Oman coast, through the protection and guidance of U.S. forces.

It is not yet clear if the most recent attacks on tankers around the strait will cause a notable drop in exports as ship operators recoil from the risk. Regardless, the U.S. military effort is a costly endeavor that experts say can’t last forever.

Before the Riyadh airport came under attack, an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq had already targeted a critical Saudi pipeline, which the kingdom was using to export oil instead of going through the Strait of Hormuz.

All told, the rebound in crude exports masks headwinds that could keep prices elevated, oil executives and analysts say. The benchmark global oil price was trading at about $104 a barrel on Monday, up from just under $70 on the eve of the war.

“We are in a permanently changed energy world right now,” said David L. Goldwyn, a former State Department energy envoy. “We are entering an age of prolonged insecurity.”

And the world’s crude cushions are being drained. The use of reserves of unrefined petroleum held by oil producers and governments has helped stabilize the market. Dozens of countries came together in March for the largest-ever coordinated release of stockpiles. But those reserves are beginning to have limited effect, in part because the world’s capacity to refine oil is stretched to the max.

The price of diesel has become a global flashpoint. Diesel is essential to global commerce, and a dearth of refineries has driven its price to record highs in many parts of the world, including the United States. Facing political pressure, President Trump has allowed imports of diesel from Russia, undercutting American sanctions for a measure that experts say will have a negligible impact on global prices.

The world’s reserves have reached “scarily thin” levels, Amin Nasser, the chief executive of Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s national oil company, said at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London last week.

In another potential weight on the energy market, there are signs that China, the world’s biggest buyer of oil, is starting to buy more again. Earlier in the war, China had slashed its imports to, at the lowest point, around 7.1 million barrels a day from about 11.6 million barrels.

And Iranian crude — 90 percent of which once went to China — has virtually disappeared from the market since the United States imposed a naval blockade on the country’s exports.

Oil executives say they expect the turmoil in the oil market to last well into next year if not longer.

“I think it is ⁠going to be bedlam for the bulk of the end of the year and maybe 2027,” Tengku Muhammad Taufik, the chief executive of Petronas, Malaysia’s state-owned oil and gas company, said last week.

For decades, the Strait of Hormuz was the most effective commercial route to send crude east across the Indian Ocean to Asian markets. Countries like Kuwait and Iraq used it for virtually all of their oil exports, while Saudi Arabia used it for about 80 percent.

When Iran effectively blocked the strait in March, Saudi Arabia, the region’s largest producer, leaned heavily on its other door to the world: the Red Sea. Each day, it sent four million to five million barrels of oil through the 720-mile East-West Pipeline to deliver crude from eastern oil fields to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. From there, ships would move its oil through the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Asia.

Over the summer, the Houthi militia made that path dangerous when it threatened to effectively block any ships carrying Saudi oil. Then in September, the Houthis attacked the East-West Pipeline, forcing it to shut down temporarily.

“Ultimately, the resilience of the international system can only hold up for so long, and we’re fast moving toward that target,” said Shaikh Nawaf S. Al-Sabah, the deputy chairman and chief executive of the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation.

Mr. Al-Sabah said that before the war, Kuwait was exporting about 2.6 million barrels a day. Production has recovered to about two million barrels a day, about 75 percent of prewar levels, because more tankers are taking the risk of transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Also notable was the warp speed at which Saudi Arabia worked to fix the East-West Pipeline after it was damaged. Mr. Nasser said Aramco had more than 10 teams, each with thousands of contractors and engineers, that repaired pumping stations in a matter of days.

Yet the region clearly remains heavily exposed.

“Producers still need a safer route, they need tankers, they still need buyers who are willing to accept the risk,” said Aaron Brady, vice president of energy oil market services at S&P Global, a research firm, at an S&P energy briefing in London this month.

Mr. Brady added, “A lot of oil is getting out in the Middle East, but there’s no longer that sort of secure workaround.”

The bottom line, Mr. Brady said, is that even though oil is getting to the countries that want it, the routes are more complicated and the costs continue to rise. He called it an “improvised” system.

“The flows are improving, but I wouldn’t characterize this as a normally operating system,” he said.

item.title: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
item.description:
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded on Monday to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, two American professors, for research that has helped guide policies aimed at reducing economic volatility.

Mr. Hall is a professor at Stanford University and Mr. Woodford is a professor of political economy at Columbia University. They were awarded the prize “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” the awarding committee said.

Mr. Hall studied consumer demand and spending to develop his models, while Mr. Woodford studied the supply side of the economy, looking at the price-setting behavior of companies. Their research has helped shape a framework for politicians, central banks and others to implement timely economic policies during upturns and downturns.

They will receive 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million, split equally between them.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said their work helped to inform fiscal and monetary policy measures, by governments and central banks, that reduced volatility in economies, so that there were milder peaks and troughs.

Because of their research, “we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

Mr. Hall and Mr. Woodford have revitalized so-called stabilization policy, which was pioneered by John Maynard Keynes, the early 20th-century British economist. This year’s prize winners developed models using microeconomic foundations, a bottom-up approach that considers how the decisions of individual households and businesses affect the economy as a whole.

By doing this, they showed the importance of how real-world behavior impacts policy and why it must be taken into account alongside broad economic variables like inflation and production. A critical aspect of their models rests on the idea that households and businesses make decisions based on what they believe will happen in the future. So when governments and policymakers communicate their economic plans, they can influence people’s expectations. That in itself can help steer the economy.

Mr. Woodford said on the phone at the news conference announcing the award that he was elated. “It’s a tremendous honor,” he said. “It’s a surprise but I feel very good about it.”

He said his work was intended to “improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy,” contributing to the management of the economy as well as the public’s understanding of the economy. He added that one of the main themes of his work was helping policymakers to appreciate that it was important to understand the behavior of individuals in the market: How they make decisions about spending and what they understand about future economic policy.

“One of the key goals of trying to develop an analytical framework was not simply to use it on people,” he said. “But to also talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done.”

Consider the immediate aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, when central banks were scrambling to deal with an economic downturn. Policymakers quickly lowered interest rates but it wasn’t enough. Additional tools were developed, such as so-called forward guidance, in which central bankers made explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rates, Mr. Woodford said. “That was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward, and I think it did contribute to better stabilization,” he added.

Last year, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt shared the award for their work on how innovation drives growth. The prize was given for research that explained the relationship between technological progress and sustained economic growth that has improved living standards, health and quality of life for people around the world.

The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer and international judge, for what the committee called her efforts to uphold a system of international law that is increasingly under attack.

Anne Carson, a Canadian poet and essayist, was awarded the prize for literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”

The prize for chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for solving a longstanding mystery about mirror images in molecules.

Francis Halzen was awarded the prize in physics for pioneering a telescope that paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.

The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discovery of a transformative neuroscience tool that may one day lead to a treatment for blindness.

item.title: Strikes Put Saudi Arabia’s Economy Under Pressure
item.description:
Andrew here. We’re tracking the fallout from the latest attacks on Saudi Arabia, especially on its main airport — including whether the U.S. will join Saudi retaliatory strikes and whether the violence will deter attendees from this month’s F.I.I. conference. We’re also analyzing the blowback to President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel sales.

Also, pay attention to an essay by Satya Nadella of Microsoft published over the weekend about building A.I. systems that prioritize human verification over blind trust. He argues that relying on human oversight is crucial for safety but also says it creates a verification tax — a concept we highlighted on Saturday — that could significantly offset A.I.’s promised productivity gains.

Saudi officials were defiant on Monday after a series of devastating attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia of Yemen, whose government Saudi Arabia backs. The violence included strikes over the weekend on the airport in Riyadh, the capital, that have killed at least 14 people.

Government leaders tried to show that it was business as usual, including by going forward with a major energy conference. But the violence raises questions about how the country’s core industries will cope — and what that might mean for global markets.

The latest:

The Saudi civil aviation authority said on Monday that operations at the airport, King Khalid International, remained suspended during work ensuring “safety and operational readiness.”

The authority said that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the airport attack on Sunday and that 11 were injured. A strike on Saturday killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds, the Saudi authorities said.

Saudi Arabia risks being further entangled in the war. The military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted missiles and drones aimed at Saudi Arabia and promised a “decisive” response.

But the assault on Saturday was the single deadliest in more than a decade on Saudi Arabia, and it followed a recent attack on a facility owned by Aramco, the Saudi-controlled oil giant.

“The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, said in a speech opening the World Petroleum Congress.

The country has been determined to show that it will continue both to provide energy security and to proceed with major international events. Those include the headline conference for the Future Investment Initiative Institute, a forum nicknamed “Davos of the Desert” that is scheduled to take place in Riyadh this month and is to feature top global C.E.O.s like Jamie Dimon of JPMorgan Chase and Larry Fink of BlackRock.

But there are still major disruptions:

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, briefly surpassed $106 a barrel this morning and remains near its highest point in two weeks.

Hundreds of Saudi-bound flights were canceled. A number of governments, including the United States’, warned travelers to reconsider travel to the country.

Several C.E.O.s of major oil companies, including ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP, withdrew from the energy conference, according to The Times.

Amid questions about whether the F.I.I. conference would go on, the institute said on Sunday that it would proceed, with “comprehensive security measures” in place at airports and hotels.

The bigger picture: The Houthi attacks have struck at the ambitions of Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, to remake his country into a hub not only for oil but for business and tourism, too.

It’s unclear what President Trump is willing to do to help Saudi Arabia, a key American ally, to confront the Houthis, who so far have refrained from attacking U.S. ships in the region.

The Justice Department questions TV networks over their coverage of the White House. Federal prosecutors on Friday began investigating whether five networks violated federal antitrust laws by collectively suspending their pooled coverage of President Trump after he barred CNN reporters from the White House. The move is the latest in the administration’s ongoing pressure on the press.

The E.U. caps imports of Chinese hybrid cars. The bloc and China agreed to limit the number of imports to 350,000 cars in the first year of a four-year deal. Brussels has been trying to reduce a trade deficit that exceeds $1.1 billion a day while avoiding a full-blown trade war. The deal still must be approved by E.U. member states.

Elon Musk has backed Republicans with more than $276 million since July. He gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, a major super PAC, and $76 million to America PAC, which he founded to improve turnout among Republican voters. His contributions make him the largest known donor in the midterms.

Another conflict is weighing on energy markets as traders gauge the seriousness of President Trump’s declaration of an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine.

Trump appeared to hope that a pause in fighting would help lower soaring diesel prices before the midterm elections. But the combatants in the war have not confirmed that there is such a deal, and lawmakers in Washington pushed back.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine accused Russia of breaking the cease-fire. At a security conference in Warsaw on Monday, Zelensky said that “Russia launched a targeted strike” on Ukrainian power and gas structures overnight.

That, Zelensky said, came hours after Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday that “effective immediately there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE” between Russia and Ukraine. Trump added, “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

“For now, this is Putin’s answer to Trump,” Zelensky said in an online address, referring to the strikes and to Vladimir Putin, Russia’s autocratic leader.

The context: The declaration, which followed the White House’s lifting of sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, appeared to take Zelensky by surprise.

But it followed weeks of complaints by Trump about Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, which have put Moscow under increasing economic pressure. Trump has blamed those strikes for the elevated diesel prices.

Zelensky, facing the prospect of a clampdown on arms from the U.S., said that Ukraine would be “ready to respect an energy cease-fire if Russia is ready to do the same.”

It’s unclear how much Trump’s move will affect fuel prices. The average price of diesel drifted down to $6.28 a gallon in the U.S. after his social media post.

But analysts said that the effect of Russian exports on diesel prices would be minimal at best. The amount that Russia would supply now would be the equivalent of about three-quarters of what the U.S. uses in a day.

Trump is facing pushback even from congressional Republicans. A bipartisan group of seven senators pushed back against Trump’s move to temporarily lift sanctions on Moscow in order to import Russian diesel.

The U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” the group wrote. “The administration must immediately reverse course.” It said that a 2022 law banned Russian energy imports to the U.S.

Worth noting: Scott Bessent said at his confirmation hearing for Treasury secretary in January 2025 that he believed that the sanctions on Russia at the time were not enough and that “the previous administration was worried about raising U.S. energy prices during an election season.”

The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was just announced, and its winners — two American economists whose work helps guide policies aimed at reducing economic volatility — underscore a key challenge facing central banks.

Who won on Monday: Stanford’s Robert Hall and Columbia’s Michael Woodford, who will split a $1.2 million prize.

Their research focuses on “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” with Hall studying economic demand and Woodford looking at supply and at companies’ price-setting behavior.

Their work shows how individual households and businesses affect the broader economy — and how they’re influenced by forward-looking pronouncements by governments and central banks, according to the announcement from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the prize.

The Financial Times’s Alphaville called Hall “the unofficial king of U.S. recession-calling for much of the past half-century” and Woodford “probably the most famous New Keynesian economist” around.

From the academy’s citation: The economic models from Hall and Woodford “have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.”

The caveat: Forward guidance has fallen out of favor in recent years in the face of new supply shocks, The Wall Street Journal notes.

And Kevin Warsh, the Fed chairman, has said he would move away from such tools, potentially risking more economic volatility, at least in the short term.

SpaceX’s head of artificial intelligence infrastructure, Michael Nicolls, said last week that the company would put data centers in orbit beginning next year as Google, Blue Origin, China and others race to build space-based computing facilities for A.I.

But the breakup of a Soviet-era weather satellite last week underscores a real risk to tech companies’ space plans: growing amounts of “space junk,” Vivienne Walt reports.

SpaceX is moving ahead with its plans. The company intends “to take A.I. compute off of Earth and put it into space,” Nicolls, who leads SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network, told a gathering of governments, scientists and investors last week in Turkey.

SpaceX’s orbital data centers are expected to dwarf Starlink, which now operates 60 percent of the world’s active satellites.

A recent “debris-generating event” highlighted the dangers of space junk. LeoLabs, which tracks satellites and orbital debris, said last week that a decades-old satellite appeared to have suffered an incident that “resulted in an estimated tens of fragments that may pose a threat to surrounding spacecraft.”

The growing amount of junk could cause accidents. Analysts fear that a collision in an increasingly crowded low-earth orbit could knock out communications crucial to global finance.

The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, which tracks major economies, estimated last month that nearly $200 billion worth of business is exposed to space debris, with risks rising fast.

A lot of close calls: Nicolls said SpaceX conducted a thousand “collision-avoidance maneuvers” a day, about one every 90 seconds. On the chances of a serious incident, he said, “the law of large numbers says if it can happen, it will happen.”

The European Space Agency warned last month that space was overcrowded and that “active debris removal is required.”

Companies are entering the space-cleanup business. Astroscale, a space-servicing company, has a contract with Eutelsat OneWeb, a European broadband service, to move one of its satellites next year to a lower orbit, where it will burn up. Astroscale will use new technology to allow its spacecraft to dock with the satellite.

“The orbital environment is becoming more cluttered and contested,” Andrew Faiola, Astroscale’s commercial vice president, told DealBook.

As for SpaceX, Nicolls said the company planned to push its expired orbital data centers deep into space, effectively to exist there forever. (Starlink brings its satellites closer to Earth to burn up in the atmosphere.)

Deals

Amazon is said to be in talks to buy Decart, a start-up that helps developers switch between artificial intelligence chips, for about $7 billion. (WSJ)

Hedge funds are buying up legal claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. (Bloomberg)

Politics, policy and regulation

“At Davos, Kimberly Guilfoyle Boasted of Private Jet Trips, Luxury Stays” (WSJ)

The sell-off in bonds could mean that central banks will not need to raise rates. But China’s heavy debt burden may make it hard for Beijing to offer more stimulus to the country’s sputtering economy. (Bloomberg, FT)

Best of the rest

Here’s what recipients of universal basic income programs, which have been promoted as a solution for job losses tied to artificial intelligence, spent their money on. (NYT)

“America’s EV Downturn Hides a Silver Lining: Charging Is Quietly Getting Better” (WSJ)

item.title: Europeans Have a Love-Hate Relationship With Chinese Cars
item.description:
BYD, China’s dominant maker of electric vehicles, aims to open so many outlets in Germany that no one has to travel more than 20 minutes to buy one of its cars. One of its Chinese rivals, Xiaomi, sees Germany as the foundation of its European expansion plans, after selling 700,000 cars back home.

Germany is the birthplace of the automobile and the home of Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz. These days, it is also a top destination for Chinese companies selling cars at a considerable discount to European vehicles.

“Customers don’t care if it’s a Chinese car or a German car,” said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a German auto analyst and former executive at Porsche and other companies. What they do care about, he said, is the price.

Shut out of the United States by tariffs, Chinese automakers have focused on other overseas markets — and Europe is a prime target. Low-cost Chinese car brands are enticing customers across the continent as surging gasoline prices drive interest in electric vehicles. Chinese cars account for about one in every 10 cars sold in Europe, up from one in 100 five years ago.

Chinese brands are rapidly gaining ground on leaders like Volkswagen. BYD’s sales in Europe have more than doubled this year. Sales of another popular Chinese manufacturer, Chery, have grown even faster. The company’s Jaecoo 7, known as the “Temu Range Rover” in a nod to the Chinese bargain-shopping app, was Britain’s best-selling vehicle in September. Xiaomi plans to add to the competition after teaming up with eight dealers in Germany.

It’s a love-hate relationship, however. Consumers increasingly want to buy Chinese cars. Policymakers are trying to stem the flow. The European Union reached a deal with Beijing on Friday that European officials said could halve the number of hybrid gasoline-electric cars that China sends to the bloc in the next four years.

The agreement could help ease the pain for European carmakers, though much about implementation remains unclear. Cheaper imports from China are threatening the industry, which contributes about 7 percent of the E.U.’s economic output. The E.U. industry chief, Stéphane Séjourné, has warned that the sector is in “mortal danger.” Germany’s auto industry group has predicted the loss of up to 225,000 jobs by 2035.

The E.U. has faced growing pressure to impose tougher measures to shield industries from what companies see as unfair competition. Left unchecked, Chinese carmakers could triple their share of the European auto market to as much as 30 percent by 2035, said Harald Hendrikse, a managing director at Citi Research.

In taking on China, Europe faces a conundrum: How can the region protect its industries while keeping prices affordable? Efforts to insulate the sector would come with a cost.

“There’s no free lunch in protectionism,” said David Bailey, a professor and industrial policy expert at University of Birmingham. “European and British automakers may gain some breathing room, but consumers could face higher prices and less choice, especially at the lower end of the market.”

For example, one proposal being considered would steer public spending toward European companies, prioritizing battery cells made in the region. But such a rule could raise the price of an electric car by 2,100 euros, or more than $2,300, according to researchers at Bruegel, a think tank in Brussels.

“Who will potentially lose from all of this?” asked Simone Tagliapietra, a deputy director at Bruegel. “I would say the middle class. They need to buy cars, right? And pushing up the cost with such provisions might be costly and even prevent them from accessing technology that, given the current energy crisis, is existentially important for Europeans.”

In 2024, the European Union imposed tariffs as high as 45 percent on Chinese electric cars to try to counter Beijing’s subsidies. But the bloc spared hybrid vehicles, which were then still a small segment of the market. Chinese manufacturers pivoted, boosting exports of hybrids, which are subject to only a 10 percent tariff.

Chinese hybrids have since poured into Europe, accounting for more than a fifth of the category’s total sales and pushing policymakers to consider wider trade restrictions. In Poland, Hungary and Romania, Chinese companies have gained more than half of the plug-in hybrid market, according to Dataforce, which tracks the auto sector.

History shows restricting supplies of those Chinese cars would probably increase prices, which over time could benefit the country’s manufacturers in Europe. In 2013, China agreed to reduce the number of solar panels that it shipped to Europe. In turn, Chinese manufacturers raised prices, pulling in larger profits that they could invest in research and new factories.

Today China dominates the world’s solar industry.

Chinese companies have their eye on the long term, seeing this period as a “bridge” toward making cars on European soil, said Matthias Schmidt, an industry analyst in Germany. He pointed to Leapmotor’s production partnership with Stellantis and BYD’s plan to produce cars in Hungary.

Chinese companies still see significant opportunity in Europe, even if new trade measures slow their advance. Spain is among the countries where they have seen strong demand and taken advantage of an increasing appetite for electric and hybrid vehicles. Electric cars have caught up with gas-powered vehicles, and electrics and hybrids together make up more than two thirds of the European market.

At the end of last year, Spain had about 600 dealerships selling Chinese brands. By the end of 2026, that number will likely grow to 1,000, according to Faconauto, a dealership association in Madrid. The market share of Chinese brands in Spain has risen fivefold in three years to about 15 percent, led by BYD and MG, the iconic British automaker now owned by a Chinese state-run company.

“For the Spanish people, this is very good,” said Marta Blázquez, Faconauto’s president.

Chinese brands have retained a significant edge on price compared with their European peers, though the gap has narrowed from a discount of as much as 30 percent in recent years, she said. The Center for European Policy Analysis in February estimated that the average starting price for a BYD electric vehicle in Europe ranged from €30,000 to €45,000, compared with prices closer to €50,000 for European E.V.s.

In Germany, even though Chinese car brands remain smaller players, they’re growing quickly. BYD said it planned to expand to as many as 300 dealerships by the end of the year. After more than doubling in 2025, sales of Chinese cars in Germany have continued to surge this year, according to Inovev, a consulting firm in Paris.

Stefan Bratzel, director of the Center of Automotive Management in Germany, invoked Frank Sinatra in explaining the importance of the country for Chinese car companies. The way they see it, “if you can make it there, you can make it anywhere.”

item.title: How American Retirees on Different Incomes Rely on Social Security
item.description:
If Congress doesn’t act, more than 60 million Americans could see their Social Security income drop by nearly a quarter in six years.

That’s when Social Security’s retirement trust fund is expected to run dry, and incoming revenue would be enough to pay only 78 percent benefits, reducing every retiree’s paycheck by 22 percent.

The program, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed into law in 1935 during the Great Depression, is not in danger of completely running out of money. While lawmakers have long known they would need to move to close that gap — through tax increases, benefit cuts or some combination — they have been slow to act on this politically charged topic.

But the window is closing.

Many of the lawmakers being elected in the coming midterms will probably be entrusted with drafting reform packages, and they will need to contemplate crucial questions: Who will absorb the costs of any changes to shore up the program, and what will the consequences be? Will people be less prepared for retirement as a result?

Procrastination has been costly, making these decisions now more difficult. Even some Republicans, who often resist any tax increases, have recently proposed raising the income ceiling on payroll taxes, the dedicated tax that finances the program, so that wealthier households contribute more.

“Any serious Social Security reform package should be scored on what it does to household retirement outcomes, not only on what it does to trust-fund balances,” said Jack VanDerhei, director of retirement research at Morningstar’s Center for Retirement & Policy Studies.

The details of any fix-it plan are crucial given the program’s extraordinary reach, potentially affecting tens of millions of working Americans, as well as future retirees and current ones — many of whom lean heavily on the program.

Just how heavily do they lean on it?

To address that question, we looked at four hypothetical households — two singles, two married couples — with different income levels and resources to illustrate the role that Social Security plays in their financial lives, a topic we’ll continue to closely track in the year ahead.

In each illustration, individuals are 64 years old and plan to retire and file for Social Security at 67, the age at which they qualify for a full retirement benefit. All analyses were run by Mr. VanDerhei of Morningstar.

Social Security is often a primary source of income for the lowest-income Americans, according to other analyses.

In this case, a single man who earned $34,000 a year, on average, over his working life is one of the roughly half of households across the country that have no money in retirement accounts to draw on.

In this case, a single worker earned about $75,000, on average, over her career. That puts her monthly Social Security benefit at $2,548, which accounts for the vast majority of her monthly income because she has just $20,000 in retirement savings (generating about $70 a month), like households with similar earnings.

About three-quarters of similarly situated households also own their own homes; the median household holds $137,000 in home equity.

With pensions fading and ever-rising costs — health care, housing, college — continuously pushed onto families, Social Security has served as a stabilizer during retirees’ most vulnerable years. Should the stock market plunge on the eve of your retirement, damaging savings at the most inopportune time, Social Security remains unaffected.

Even households with solid income and savings need to stow away and accumulate substantial sums to draw even a modest income — one that must last for potentially several decades.

That $1 million savings milestone? It will typically generate $40,000 a year (adjusted upward for inflation in future years).

Each worker here earned $75,000, on average, over the course of their careers, for a combined total of $150,000. Retirement savings of $171,700 provide $572 in monthly income. Most households like theirs also own homes, with the median household holding $251,800 in home equity. A little more than a quarter also hold stocks, bonds or mutual funds outside retirement accounts.

This couple collectively earned about $261,000 a year — one spouse earned at least the maximum amount subject to Social Security payroll taxes each year, which works out to an average of about $186,000 over this spouse’s career; the other worker earned $75,000 on average.

Their retirement savings of $435,000 could generate monthly income of $1,450. Most similar households own their homes; the median household holds $400,600 in home equity. About half hold stocks, bonds or mutual funds outside retirement accounts.

Many retirees report feeling reliant on Social Security.

But it’s more than just a feeling: Among beneficiaries 60 and older in the middle of a five-rung income ladder, where median household income was projected at about $90,900 in 2024, Social Security made up 38 percent of household income on average, according to the Social Security Administration’s MINT model, which uses administrative earnings and benefits records to make projections.

Those in the next-highest rung, with median household income of $152,300, leaned on Social Security for a quarter of their income, on average, while the group just below the middle relied on it for 56 percent.

Other studies have shown that roughly 42 percent of households rely on Social Security for at least half of their retirement income.

The program is more than just an inflation-adjusted insurance policy against running out of money in retirement — it also provides disability, survivor and family benefits. When so much of our financial lives rides on luck, timing and our collective human vulnerability, this social contract has persevered.

Assumptions and sources for illustrations

— Each example pairs a Social Security benefit calculated for a hypothetical worker born in 1962 who claims at 67 in 2029, with the retirement savings of real households near retirement with similar wages. The low and middle earners’ pay follows a career pattern based on actual workers’ earnings, rising with national wages; the higher earner earns at least the maximum amount subject to Social Security tax each year. Career-average earnings are stated in 2026 wage levels. Benefits are in 2026 dollars adjusted for inflation.

— The reduced check assumes the retirement trust fund is depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, as projected in the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, after which about 78 percent of scheduled benefits would initially be payable. It is an illustrative proportional reduction, not a benefit estimate provided by the Social Security Administration.

— Retirement savings figures are medians from the Federal Reserve’s 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, adjusted for inflation, for comparable households headed by someone age 55 to 64 in 2022. They are not projections; balances could rise or fall with contributions, withdrawals and investment returns.

— Retirement savings include individual retirement accounts, like Roth I.R.A.s, and employer plans such as 401(k)s and 403(b)s. Income from savings assumes a 4 percent annual withdrawal. It excludes pensions, earnings, home equity and other assets like stocks, bonds, mutual funds and annuities held outside retirement accounts. All income figures are before taxes.

— All data and analysis are from Jack VanDerhei, director of retirement research at Morningstar’s Center for Retirement & Policy Studies.
